parsed.attack: Camera phones have been in every garage for fifteen years and no restorer pays for teardown documentation - they photograph and bag, and that solution costs twenty pence and works. This audience is time-rich and money-poor by construction (a single long project bike is a hobby that consumes evenings deliberately), so labour saved has no price, and the value only materialises at reassembly three to six months later, meaning nobody can feel the benefit at the moment of purchase. The addressable set is not 'home-garage motorcycle restorers' but the intersection of that group with people who already own Ray-Ban Display glasses and will wear them under garage lighting with oily hands - plausibly a few thousand people worldwide in year one, with no channel. The only cited evidence is two head-worn products that failed, which is evidence against demand being reframed as evidence that demand was merely mispriced.
parsed.strongest_defence: Hands-free capture is categorically different from phone capture when your hands are covered in oil - the reason people do not document teardowns is not that they do not want the record but that picking up a phone mid-operation is the one thing you cannot do - and restorers are a forum-dense community with proven willingness to spend hundreds on single-purpose tools, so 500 units at $30 is a trivially low bar inside an install base that is growing.
parsed.verdict_reason: Fifteen years of free camera phones producing no paid market for teardown records is strong behavioural evidence the pain is tolerated, though hands-free capture is a genuine change in the cost of the behaviour.
